lines: Here's something weird. You can do absolutely nothing with your money, and it still shrinks.
Your grandpa probably paid about two dollars for a movie ticket. Today it's around eleven. The movie didn't get five times better. The dollar got weaker.
That's inflation: prices across the whole economy creeping up, so each dollar buys a little less. Economists call that losing purchasing power.

To measure it, the government tracks a basket of everyday stuff, like food, rent, gas and haircuts. That's the Consumer Price Index, or CPI. If the basket costs four percent more than last year, inflation is four percent.
Now the most important idea in this lesson: nominal versus real. Nominal is the raw number of dollars. Real is what those dollars can actually buy.
Say your boss gives you a two percent raise, but prices went up four percent. Nominally, you got a raise. Really, you got a pay cut.
Same with savings. Cash in a drawer earns zero. If inflation is three percent, you're quietly losing three percent a year. That's why people invest.
The other big number is GDP, gross domestic product. It's the value of everything a country makes in a year. Consumer spending, business investment, government purchases, plus exports minus imports.
When GDP grows faster than prices, the economy is really growing. When real GDP shrinks for a while, that's a recession.
So whenever you see a number about money, ask one question. Is that nominal, or real? That one question puts you ahead of most people.
